 ## Search results
HSTU already has a strong sampled-softmax precedent: Meta’s [official configuration](https://github.com/meta-recsys/generative-recommenders/blob/main/configs/ml-1m/hstu-sampled-softmax-n128-final.gin) uses 128 negatives, L2-normalized embeddings and temperature 0.05. These are starting points, not established Amazon optima. [Wu et al., 2024](https://wujcan.github.io/papers/tois-ssm.pdf) show that sampled softmax emphasizes hard negatives through its gradients; temperature controls this emphasis, with excessively low temperatures allowing a few difficult negatives to dominate. Thus, larger negative pools and temperature tuning are useful controlled experiments before adding explicit mining.

Harder negatives can improve discrimination but also amplify false negatives: an unobserved, highly scored item may actually interest the user. [R²NS, WWW 2026](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) reports early-training failures from aggressive mining and supports uniform-negative warm-up followed by progressively harder sampling. It discusses stochastic selection among top-ranked candidates to reduce deterministic hardest-item selection. A [2024 sequential-recommendation comparison](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) also finds sampler-dependent popularity trade-offs; popularity-based sampling does not universally improve aggregate accuracy.

Practical hypothesis for this task: retain one HSTU per category; compare multi-negative softmax with 64–256 negatives and temperatures 0.05–0.2, then test a warm-up followed by mixed uniform and stochastic hard negatives scored by that same model. Exclude padding, the target and known training-history positives; never consult held-out labels when sampling. These ranges are proposed experiments, not published Electronics-specific findings. Select using fixed four-category macro validation HR@10, inspecting Electronics separately. Larger training margins against easy negatives alone do not establish better ranking.

---

HSTU already provides a natural temporal mechanism: relative position/time attention bias alongside SiLU-based attention and multiplicative feature gating. Its time bias can learn which elapsed-time ranges matter without imposing uniform decay. The gate is feature interaction, however, not an explicitly supervised estimate that a need has been fulfilled. [Original HSTU paper, 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.17152v3). FuXi-α (WWW 2025) motivates separating temporal, positional and semantic attention channels; this supports richer temporal conditioning but does not establish purchase-completion detection. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03036).

T-RoPE (September 2026 preprint) extends HSTU with continuous timestamp rotations, learnable temporal coefficients, multiscale frequencies and calendar-sensitive encoding. Authors report improvements over HSTU with time-relative attention bias, suggesting elapsed time and periodicity provide complementary signals. Its shifted-query training uses next-event timestamps and inference uses current query time, so benchmark adoption requires checking which query-time information is actually available; held-out event timestamps must not be assumed available. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.30576v1).

A compatible experiment is a jointly trained, content-conditioned recency gate inside the existing causal HSTU: condition historical contributions on bucketed/log time gaps and the current hidden state, while retaining access to older preferences. Compare positional bias alone, temporal bias, and temporal bias plus gating using the fixed macro validation HR@10. This gate is a proposed hypothesis, not a demonstrated finding from these sources. Interaction histories cannot identify fulfilled needs directly; any benefit would establish predictive temporal adaptation, not verified purchase completion. Keep one network/checkpoint per category and use only timestamps available at prediction.

[HSTU (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17152) supports heterogeneous feature representations within sequential transduction, providing a basis for adding content while retaining its backbone. [HLLM (2024)](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.12740v1) jointly optimizes an item-text encoder and a user-sequence encoder through next-item prediction; it explicitly evaluates training both from scratch, although pretrained initialization performs better. Transferable idea: compress each title/description into one learned item vector before sequential modeling. HLLM itself uses a different backbone, so its architecture and reported gains cannot be directly attributed to HSTU.

[AttrFormer (KDD 2025)](https://www.amazon.science/publications/learning-attribute-as-explicit-relation-for-sequential-recommendation) models attributes as explicit item relations rather than relying entirely on blended ID/attribute embeddings. A task-compatible hypothesis is to derive lexical tokens only from supplied titles/descriptions—model numbers, connector names, dimensions, format markers—and learn their embeddings jointly with item IDs inside one HSTU network. A small randomly initialized text encoder, field embeddings, and a learned residual gate could supply shared input/candidate representations under one next-item loss. These are proposed adaptations, not established HSTU results; matching lexical attributes does not establish actual product compatibility.
